# Notes on Judges 7

**What I found and what's missing:**
- **Traditional reading:** well covered. Main sources are Guzik (Enduring Word), Ellicott, Gill, Pulpit, Keil & Delitzsch, Spurgeon and Precept Austin.
- **Protestant differences:** I found no real split between denominations on this chapter. The one live debate is over the meaning of the drinking test (vv. 5–6), and it cuts across traditions rather than following them.
- **Not found:** NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey, and anything from newadvent, catholic.com or oca.org. I also found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter. Those are left out.
- **Early Church:** the only early-Church reading I found is Origen, and only as reported by Guzik and Clarke, not from his own text.

---

**v. 1**
- Ellicott notes that many people in Scripture have two names. He says "beside" is better read "above," because it would have been foolish and dangerous to encamp on the plain. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-7.html
- Ellicott: Harod means "trembling," which matches the frightened men of v. 3. He identifies the spring with Ain Jalûd and the hill of Moreh with Little Hermon. (same URL)
- Precept Austin: Jerubbaal means "Baal will contend," so the name was a standing rebuke to Baal-worship. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_7_commentary

**v. 2**
- Guzik: 32,000 men could still have claimed the credit as plucky underdogs. God reduces the army from 32,000 to 300 not out of weakness but so victory will clearly belong to Him alone. He links this to Zechariah 4:6 and Psalm 20:7. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-7/
- Ellicott cross-references Deuteronomy 8:17. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-7.html
- Precept Austin: God often cuts back our resources so that we depend wholly on Him. The temptation to take a share of the glory is still with us today. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_7_commentary

**v. 3**
- Ellicott: sending the fearful home follows Deuteronomy 20:8, which rests on the observation that cowardice spreads through an army. He adds that many of those who left probably joined the later pursuit. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-7.html
- Guzik: the men could see the Midianite army, which explains why so many were afraid. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-7/

**v. 4**
- Ellicott: the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) translates "I will try them" as "I will purge them," as gold is purged of dross. He calls this the literal sense of the word. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-7.html

**vv. 5–6 (the main debate)**
- **They were the most alert.** Guzik suggests those who cupped water to their mouths stayed alert even while drinking. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-7/ Keil & Delitzsch see them as the bravest, men who would not stop to kneel before battle. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/7-6.htm
- **They were the cowards.** Ellicott reports that Josephus held the opposite view, those to be the cowards who lapped the water hastily. Theodoret thought God's help showed more clearly because the most cowardly men were chosen. Ellicott himself prefers the self-control reading. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-7.html
- **Kneeling meant idolatry.** Ellicott reports that the Jewish commentator Rashi took those who knelt to be secret idolaters who had "bowed the knee to Baal." (same URL)
- **It wasn't about character at all.** Gill says it is hard to tell. He suggests the test may simply have been a way to cut numbers: most men were very thirsty and would kneel for a long drink. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/7-7.htm Precept Austin warns against reading in some weighty spiritual lesson that God never put there. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_7_commentary
- **A modern scholar's view.** Constable cites D. Daube (1956), who suggested the dog-like lapping symbolises lapping up the enemy's blood. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/7-5.html

**v. 7**
- JFB: Gideon's steady faith in God's promise is why he is so highly commended (Heb 11:32). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/7-7.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary compares 1 Samuel 14:6. Keil & Delitzsch note that God gave the promise before the command, to make obeying easier. (same URL)
- Guzik: Israel's army was now under 1% of its original size, with about 400 Midianites for every Israelite. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-7/

**v. 8**
- Ellicott: most ancient versions say the 300 took the provisions and horns of the departing men, which explains how each had his own horn. The jars may have been the provision jars. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-7.html

**vv. 9–11**
- Guzik sees God's tender mercy here: God meets Gideon's fear with reassurance instead of leaving him to manage alone. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-7/
- Ellicott relates the overheard words to the Jewish idea of a "voice from heaven" (the Bath Kol), where chance words heard after watching for a sign are taken as divine guidance. He takes "the armed men" to mean the outposts or sentries. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-7.html

**v. 12**
- Ellicott: camels were the main wealth of the desert tribes. The "host" was probably a migrating people with many camp followers, not only soldiers. (same URL)

**v. 13**
- Ellicott: Israel had been raided into poverty and lived on barley bread. Josephus calls barley the poorest of grains. The tent struck was probably the royal tent. (same URL)
- Spurgeon calls barley cake the emblem of a thing despised. He stresses God's providence in arranging the dream and its timing so exactly, and that God uses despised means. https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons31.lviii.html
- Spurgeon also gently rebukes Gideon for taking more comfort from a dream than from God's own word. https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/sermons/the-dream-of-barley-cake/

**v. 14**
- Ellicott: the enemy's instant interpretation shows how much they dreaded Israel's God. It also echoed the promise Gideon had already received in v. 9. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-7.html
- Spurgeon: the enemy already feared Gideon, and the powers of evil are weaker than they look. https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/sermons/the-dream-of-barley-cake/
- Precept Austin counts this as the fifth time God promised deliverance into Gideon's hand. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_7_commentary

**v. 15**
- Ellicott: the Hebrew word for "interpretation" literally means "its breaking," like cracking open a nut. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-7.html
- Kelly: Gideon worships as he hears; his confidence is in the Lord. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/7-13.html

**v. 16**
- Ellicott: dividing a force into three was a common tactic. Hearing 300 horns, Midian would assume 300 companies were attacking. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-7.html
- JFB: the pitchers were empty so they could hide the torches, and earthenware so they would break easily. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/judges-7.html
- **Link to 2 Corinthians 4:7 (light in clay jars):**
  - JFB treats Gideon's pitchers as a "type" of Paul's clay jars. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/2Cr/2Cr_004.cfm
  - Bible.org argues that when believers are broken by suffering, the gospel's light shines out, as from Gideon's jars. https://bible.org/seriespage/4-distinguishing-contents-container-2-cor-47-15

**vv. 17–18**
- Guzik: the plan isn't said to come from a revelation, but Gideon was Spirit-filled (6:34), so the supernatural worked naturally through him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-7/
- Ellicott: the Hebrew is literally "For the LORD and for Gideon"; "sword" is supplied from v. 20 and better left out. Naming Gideon was meant to terrify an enemy that already feared him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-7.html
- Guzik likewise says the cry was not the result of pride. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-7/

**v. 19**
- Ellicott: Israel then divided the night into three watches, so the middle watch began around 10 p.m., during the enemy's first sleep. The attack came amid the confusion of the changing guard. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-7.html

**v. 20**
- Ellicott: with their hands full, the men were nearly defenceless. He cites similar ruses in ancient history (Hannibal's torches, trumpets used by Greek commanders). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-7.html
- The BibleHub study notes read the torch in the weaker left hand as a sign that the strength comes from God. https://biblehub.com/study/judges/7-20.htm
- Precept Austin applies it to Christians: break the pitcher and let your light shine, then sound the trumpet. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_7_commentary
- **Early Church allegory:** Guzik reports that Origen made the 300 a picture of gospel preachers, their trumpets the preaching of Christ crucified, and their torches holy living. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-7/ Clarke places this in Origen's ninth homily on Judges. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/7-20.html

**v. 21**
- Ellicott: the Midianites' cries were either wailing or confused shouted orders. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-7.html

**v. 22**
- Ellicott: compare 2 Chronicles 20 and 1 Samuel 14. The rout stayed in Israel's memory (Isaiah 9:4, 10:26; Psalm 83). (same URL)
- Guzik: Midian fought itself first, an illustration of being "more than conquerors" (Romans 8:37). We share the spoils of a battle Jesus won for us. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-7/

**v. 23**
- Bridgeway: the larger Israelite forces now joined the battle. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/7-24.html

**v. 24**
- The Pulpit Commentary says "the waters" were streams flowing from Ephraim's hills into the Jordan, which Midian had to cross. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/7-24.htm
- Barnes: Gideon had not yet dared to summon the powerful tribe of Ephraim. This sets up the quarrel in 8:1. (same URL)
- **Where was Beth-barah?** Clarke thinks it is probably the place mentioned in John 1:28. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/7-24.html Ellicott thinks it is too far south to be that place. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/7-24.htm

**v. 25**
- The Pulpit Commentary: the names mean "raven" and "wolf." The rock and the winepress were named afterwards for where the princes died (compare Isaiah 10:26). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/7-25.htm
- Ellicott: these were ordinary warrior names among nomads, not insults given by Israel. https://biblehub.com/judges/7-25.htm
- The BibleHub notes point out an irony: Gideon had hidden his grain in a winepress (6:11), and now a Midianite prince dies in one. (same URL)
